The short version

If you submit our form, we use your answers to understand your need and connect you with relevant suppliers — and we may be paid a referral fee if you go on to work with one. 1) What we collect

Information you give us. When you submit our contact form, we collect what you provide — typically your name, work email, company, application and fluid details, scale, timeline, and any message. Please don’t include confidential specifications or sensitive personal data.

Information collected automatically. Like most sites, basic technical data (IP address, browser/device type, referring page) may be collected for security and operation. This site is hosted on Blogger (Google), which may set functional cookies.

Form and storage providers. Our form and the storage behind it process your submission on our behalf so we can receive and manage your inquiry.

To understand your request, respond, and — where relevant — introduce you to suppliers who transact in these fluids. Technical data is used to keep the site secure and working. If you opt in, we may send occasional updates; you can unsubscribe anytime.

  • Suppliers, to make introductions. We may share your inquiry with relevant fluid makers, system builders, or distributors. We may receive a referral fee if you go on to work with them. We don’t vet, endorse, or guarantee any supplier.

  • Legal reasons. We may disclose information if required by law or to protect rights and safety.

Prefer we don’t share your details? Say so in the form or email us, and we’ll just answer your questions.

4) Your choices and rights

Depending on where you live, you may have rights to access, correct, or delete your information, and to opt out of its "sale" or "sharing." Because our introductions may count as sharing under those laws, you can opt out — email hello@dielectricfluid.com and note "opt out." We won’t discriminate against you for exercising these rights. You can also control cookies through your browser.

5) Retention and security

We keep inquiry information as long as needed to respond, make introductions, keep records of consent, and meet legal needs, then delete or de-identify it. We use reasonable measures to protect information, but no transmission is completely secure — please don’t send sensitive data through the form.

6) Changes and contact

We may update this policy; the date below reflects the current version. Questions or requests? Email hello@dielectricfluid.com.

About. DielectricFluid.com is an independent, vendor-neutral guide to dielectric immersion cooling fluids — for data-center operators, EV and battery engineers, and anyone choosing between the fluids that make liquid cooling possible. We explain the options in plain engineering terms, then connect people who want to transact with the right suppliers.

What this site does

Explains the chemistries and tradeoffs · tracks the fast-moving PFAS transition · organizes the supplier landscape neutrally · and connects buyers with relevant fluid makers, system builders, and distributors.

Who runs this site

DielectricFluid.com is founded, written, and maintained by Ahmad Hassan, PhD. With a background in research and engineering, Ahmad approaches this fast-changing area the same way he approaches any technical problem: every page is built from primary materials — supplier datasheets, industry and trade sources, and regulatory texts — explained in plain English, dated, and re-checked when the landscape moves. The aim is to make a genuinely technical subject understandable to a smart non-specialist.

This is an independent publisher — not a fluid maker, distributor, or system vendor. Nothing here is engineering, safety, or purchasing advice, and reading it doesn’t replace your own validation. For decisions about your own system, work with the supplier and your own engineers.

The site is free to read. We earn revenue by introducing readers to the suppliers who transact in this space — fluid makers, system builders, and distributors — and we may receive a referral fee when an introduction leads to business. Suppliers can also pay for a featured directory listing. An introduction is never an endorsement, our editorial comparisons are written independently of who pays us, and we don’t run display ads. In one sentence

A dielectric fluid is an electrically non-conductive liquid that can sit in direct contact with live electrical components — carrying heat away without causing a short circuit. That single property is what makes immersion cooling possible.

"Dielectric" simply means electrically insulating. A dielectric fluid is a liquid engineered to not conduct electricity, so it can touch energized parts safely. Ordinary water can’t do this — it conducts — which is why immersion cooling relies on specially formulated fluids instead.

The defining trick: cools the chip directly, conducts no electricity

What a good dielectric cooling fluid does

  • Insulates electrically — high dielectric strength so it won’t short live components.
  • Moves heat efficiently — good thermal conductivity and heat capacity to carry energy away.
  • Stays safe — a high flash point and, ideally, non-flammability.
  • Plays well with materials — compatible with the seals, plastics, and metals it contacts.
  • Lasts — resists oxidation and degradation over a long service life.

For how these properties trade off, see how to choose a fluid.

Where dielectric fluids are used

UseWhat the fluid does
Data centersImmersion-cools high-density servers directly, replacing air cooling
EV batteriesCools cells directly for fast charging and thermal safety
Power electronicsCools inverters, converters, and dense power modules
Transformers (legacy)Long-standing use as insulating and cooling oil — the original dielectric fluid application

The chemistries at a glance

Dielectric cooling fluids fall into four families — hydrocarbon, synthetic, ester, and fluorocarbon — each with its own balance of cost, performance, safety, and PFAS status. We break them down in fluid types.

Frequently asked

Why can’t you cool electronics with water?
Water conducts electricity, so it would short out live components on contact. Dielectric fluids are formulated to be non-conductive, which is exactly what lets them touch energized hardware safely.
Is dielectric fluid the same as coolant?
It’s a coolant with a special requirement: it must also be electrically insulating. General coolants (like water-glycol) cool well but conduct, so they’re kept separate from live parts. Dielectric fluids can contact them directly.
Are transformer oil and immersion-cooling fluid the same?
They share the dielectric principle, but immersion-cooling fluids for data centers and EVs are engineered for those specific thermal and material demands. Transformer oil is the older, commodity end of the dielectric-fluid world.

The short answer

Immersion cooling fluids come in four families: hydrocarbon (affordable baseline), synthetic (higher performance), ester (safe, bio-based, EV favorite), and fluorocarbon (top thermal performance for two-phase, but PFAS and now supply-constrained). The first three are PFAS-free.

Every dielectric immersion fluid belongs to one of four chemistry families. Each makes a different trade among cost, thermal performance, safety, material compatibility, and regulatory exposure. Here’s the neutral version of what each gives you — and gives up.

1. Hydrocarbon (mineral & GTL)

The affordable baseline · single-phase · PFAS-free

Mineral-oil and gas-to-liquid (GTL) based fluids are the most cost-effective and widely used family for single-phase data-center immersion. They cool well for most server loads and carry no PFAS. The main watch-item is oxidation over a long service life, which good additive packages address.

2. Synthetic / engineered hydrocarbon

Higher performance · single-phase · PFAS-free

Engineered for tuned viscosity and improved thermal and oxidative stability, synthetics sit above mineral oils on both performance and price. They’re a strong fit for high-density single-phase deployments where you want more margin than a basic hydrocarbon offers. Specifications vary by supplier — compare datasheets directly.

3. Ester (synthetic & natural)

Safe & bio-based · the EV favorite · PFAS-free

Esters bring a high flash point and strong safety profile, plus bio-based, environmentally cleaner options. That makes them the leading choice for EV battery immersion and for sustainability-led data centers. The key engineering question is long-life validation — proving durability over years of service.

4. Fluorocarbon (fluorinated)

Top thermal performance · two-phase · PFAS — restricted

Fluorinated fluids deliver excellent two-phase boiling performance and the lowest PUE potential, which is why they dominated high-end immersion. But they are PFAS chemistry, sit at the top of the cost range, and now face both supply disruption (the 3M Novec/Fluorinert exit) and pending restriction (the EU’s expected PFAS vote). See the Novec replacement guide.

Frequently asked

Which family is PFAS-free?
Hydrocarbon, synthetic, and ester fluids are all PFAS-free. Fluorocarbon (fluorinated) fluids are the PFAS chemistry now facing supply and regulatory pressure.
Why are fluorocarbons used at all if they’re restricted?
They deliver the best two-phase boiling performance and lowest PUE, which mattered for the most extreme heat loads. The 3M exit and pending PFAS rules are now pushing the market toward PFAS-free alternatives.
Which family should I start with?
For most single-phase data-center needs, hydrocarbon or synthetic; for EV battery immersion, ester. Start from your application and architecture — see how to choose.

The short answer

Single-phase keeps the fluid liquid and pumps it to a heat exchanger — simpler, safer, and served by PFAS-free fluids. Two-phase lets the fluid boil and condense for the highest heat-removal density and lowest PUE — but it has historically depended on fluorinated fluids now hit by the 3M exit and pending PFAS rules. For most projects today, single-phase is the lower-risk default; two-phase is for genuine extreme-density needs.

It’s the first real fork in any immersion cooling project, and it decides far more than cooling performance — it determines which fluids are even available to you, your maintenance model, and your regulatory exposure.

Fig.1 — pumped liquid versus boiling and condensing

Side by side

FactorSingle-phaseTwo-phase
How it worksFluid stays liquid, pumped to a heat exchangerFluid boils at the chip, vapor condenses and falls back
Heat-removal densityHighHighest
PUE potentialVery goodBest

PFAS statusPFAS-free options widely availableTraditionally PFAS — supply & regulatory risk
Fluid costLowerHigher
Maturity for new buildsMainstreamIn flux post-3M-exit

When each one wins

Choose single-phase when you want the lower-risk, lower-cost, PFAS-free path and your heat loads are within its (substantial) capability — which covers the large majority of data-center and many EV and power-electronics applications today.

Choose two-phase when you have genuinely extreme heat-flux requirements where boiling’s latent-heat advantage is decisive and the lowest possible PUE justifies the added complexity — and you have a credible, compliant fluid supply lined up.

The two-phase fluid problem, plainly

The fluids that made two-phase practical at scale — 3M’s Novec and Fluorinert — are discontinued, and fluorinated alternatives face the EU’s pending PFAS restriction. If you’re committing to two-phase today, your single biggest open question isn’t thermal performance — it’s securing a fluid that’s both available and compliant for the life of the system. See the Novec replacement guide.

Frequently asked

Which is better for a new data center?
For most new builds, single-phase is the lower-risk default — mature, PFAS-free, lower-cost, and capable of very strong PUE. Two-phase is reserved for the most extreme density needs where its performance edge justifies the complexity and the fluid-supply question.
Does two-phase always need PFAS fluids?
Historically the practical, widely-deployed two-phase fluids were fluorinated. PFAS-free two-phase fluids are being developed but are still emerging, so today a two-phase commitment usually means engaging closely with suppliers on fluid availability and compliance.
Can I switch phases later?
Not easily — the tank, sealing, and thermal design differ significantly. The phase choice is an architectural commitment, which is why it’s worth getting right before fluid selection.

The short answer

Choosing an immersion cooling fluid comes down to four decisions, in order: your application, single- or two-phase, PFAS exposure, and then the fluid properties that follow from those. Get the first three right and the chemistry shortlist usually picks itself.

There is no single "best" immersion fluid — only the best fit for your hardware, heat load, regulatory situation, and operating life. This guide walks the decision the way an experienced thermal engineer would, then points you to the supplier conversation with the right questions already in hand.

The decision, visualized

Fig.1 — the fluid decision, in order

The four factors, in order

1

Application sets the baseline

A hyperscale data center, a fast-charging EV battery pack, and a power-electronics enclosure have different heat profiles, safety rules, and service lives. EV programs lean heavily toward synthetic esters; data centers toward hydrocarbons and synthetics. Start here — it frames everything else. See data centers and EV cooling.

2

Single-phase or two-phase

This is the architecture fork. Single-phase keeps the fluid liquid and pumps it; two-phase lets it boil for the highest heat-removal density. Your choice narrows the fluid families before properties even enter the picture. See single vs two-phase.

3

PFAS / regulatory exposure

If you must avoid PFAS — because of where you sell or customer mandates — fluorinated two-phase fluids drop off the list, which often pushes you toward single-phase PFAS-free chemistries. This factor has become decisive since the 3M exit. See PFAS transition.

4

Then the properties that matter

Only now do the spec numbers decide between the survivors: dielectric strength, flash point, viscosity, thermal conductivity, material compatibility, oxidation stability, and cost. See fluid types for how the families compare.

The properties to actually compare

PropertyWhy it matters
Dielectric strengthThe fluid must be electrically non-conductive in direct contact with live components.
Flash pointHigher is safer. A key reason esters are favored in EVs and many hydrocarbons are engineered for high flash points.
ViscosityAffects pumping energy and how well fluid reaches hot spots, especially across temperature swings.
Thermal conductivity / heat capacityDetermines raw cooling capability per unit of flow.
Material compatibilityThe fluid contacts seals, plastics, solder, and coatings — incompatibility causes swelling or degradation over time.
Oxidation & long-life stabilityDecides service life and maintenance interval — the open question for many ester and hydrocarbon fluids.
Cost per gallonRanges widely; fluorinated fluids sit at the top, hydrocarbons at the bottom.
Take this to your supplier

Ask for the current datasheet with measured values for each property above, the material-compatibility list, the recommended service life, and the fluid’s PFAS status in writing. A supplier who can answer all of these cleanly is a supplier worth shortlisting.

Frequently asked

Is there a single best immersion fluid?
No. The best fluid is the one that fits your application, cooling architecture, regulatory exposure, and service-life needs. A fluid that’s ideal for an EV pack may be wrong for a hyperscale data center.
Which decision should I make first?
Application, then single- vs two-phase, then PFAS exposure. Those three almost always narrow the chemistry before you compare spec numbers.
How much does fluid cost?
It varies enormously — hydrocarbons are the most affordable, synthetics and esters sit in the middle, and fluorinated two-phase fluids are the most expensive, often hundreds of dollars per gallon. Total system fluid volume makes this a material line item.

The short answer

As fast charging pushes past the limits of indirect cooling, EV makers are exploring immersion — bathing battery cells directly in a dielectric fluid. Synthetic esters lead this space for their high flash point, safety profile, and PFAS-free chemistry. The open engineering question is validating fluid stability over the vehicle’s full service life.

Battery thermal management decides charging speed, safety, range, and longevity. Traditional indirect cooling — cold plates and coolant channels separated from the cells — struggles as charging rates climb, because heat has to cross materials to reach the coolant. Immersion puts a non-conductive fluid in direct contact with the cells, cooling them faster and more evenly, and adding a margin of safety against thermal runaway.

Why immersion for EVs now

Ultra-fast charging generates heat faster than indirect systems can move it, and uneven cooling shortens pack life and limits sustained charge rates. Direct immersion cooling addresses both: every cell sits in the same fluid, so temperatures stay uniform, peak heat is removed quickly, and the dielectric fluid provides an additional barrier against propagation in a thermal event.

Why synthetic esters dominate

EV fluid selection weights safety heavily, and esters fit: a high flash point, good dielectric strength, and PFAS-free bio-based options. That combination — safe, non-conductive, environmentally cleaner — is why synthetic and natural esters have become the default starting point for EV immersion programs. (See fluid types.)

The real engineering challenge

It isn’t finding a fluid that cools well — it’s proving the fluid stays stable and compatible across years of thermal cycling, vibration, and contact with pack materials. Long-life validation, not peak performance, is where EV fluid programs live or die. And because automotive fluid choices are typically locked in years before production, much of today’s activity is in qualification and design-win stages.

Frequently asked

Why esters and not hydrocarbons for EVs?
Esters bring a high flash point and strong safety profile that EV programs prioritize, plus PFAS-free bio-based options. Hydrocarbons are used in some designs, but esters have become the leading starting point for battery immersion.
Is EV immersion cooling in production yet?
It’s emerging and growing quickly. Because automotive fluid choices are locked in years before production through long validation cycles, much current activity is in design-win and qualification stages.
What’s the hardest part of fluid selection?
Long-life validation — proving the fluid stays stable and compatible with pack materials across the vehicle’s service life under real thermal and mechanical stress.

The short answer

AI is pushing rack densities past the point air can cool, and dielectric immersion fluids are how operators handle it. For most data centers the practical choice is a single-phase hydrocarbon or synthetic fluid — strong performance, PFAS-free, lower cost — with two-phase reserved for the most extreme heat densities, where the fluid supply is now constrained.

Cooling can consume a large share of a data center’s energy, and conventional air cooling runs out of headroom as rack power climbs. AI and HPC have accelerated this sharply: as racks push toward and past 100 kW — with frontier AI accelerators exceeding 1,000 W per chip — liquid cooling stops being optional. Immersion (submerging hardware directly in a non-conductive dielectric fluid) removes heat far more effectively than air and can dramatically improve PUE.

Why PUE drives the move

Air-cooled facilities average a PUE well above 1.5; immersion can reach the low 1.0s — a large cut in cooling-related energy.

Why operators are moving to immersion

Air cooling fights physics at high density: fans consume power, hot spots persist, and floor space is wasted on airflow. Immersing hardware in dielectric fluid puts the coolant in direct contact with the heat source, enabling much higher density per rack, quieter operation, near-zero cooling water use in closed-loop designs, and better energy efficiency — while the fluid’s non-conductive nature keeps live electronics safe.

Single-phase or two-phase for a data center?

This is the architectural decision that frames everything (see single vs two-phase). In short:

  • Single-phase — the mainstream data-center choice, leading installed capacity. Pumped hydrocarbon or synthetic fluid, PFAS-free, lower cost, strong PUE, fewer failure points.
  • Two-phase — the best raw efficiency for extreme density and the fastest-growing segment, but built around fluorinated fluids now facing supply and PFAS-regulation risk after the 3M exit.

What to weigh beyond thermal performance

  • Material compatibility — seals, optics, labels, and coatings all sit in the fluid.
  • Retrofit vs greenfield — immersion changes the physical facility; new builds have more freedom.
  • Maintenance model — serviceability of submerged hardware and fluid top-up over time.
  • Fluid lifecycle — oxidation stability and replacement interval affect long-run cost.
  • Compliance — PFAS exposure given where you operate and your sustainability commitments.

Frequently asked

At what density do I need liquid cooling?
As a rule of thumb, beyond roughly 100 kW per rack air cooling becomes impractical, and many AI/HPC deployments are well past that — some single-phase immersion designs support 200 kW or more per rack. The exact threshold depends on your hardware and facility.
Is immersion better than cold plate / direct-to-chip?
They’re different liquid-cooling approaches. Direct-to-chip targets the hottest components and is widely deployed; immersion cools the whole board in dielectric fluid and reaches very high density with fewer mechanical parts. The right choice depends on hardware, serviceability, and density.
Which fluid do most data centers use?
Single-phase hydrocarbon and synthetic fluids are the mainstream choice today — PFAS-free, cost-effective, and well-proven — with two-phase fluorinated fluids reserved for the most extreme densities.

The short answer

PFAS — the "forever chemicals" — include the fluorinated fluids that powered high-end two-phase immersion cooling. 3M has exited PFAS manufacturing (Novec and Fluorinert ended in 2025), and the EU is advancing a broad restriction: ECHA’s scientific committees backed it in March 2026, with the European Commission expected to propose rules around Q3 2027 and a restriction unlikely to apply before 2029. The result — fluorinated fluids now carry both supply and regulatory risk.

PFAS (per- and polyfluoroalkyl substances) are a large class of synthetic chemicals valued for stability and non-flammability — the very traits that made certain fluorinated fluids excellent dielectric coolants for two-phase immersion. Those same traits make them environmentally persistent, which is why they’re now the target of both regulation and corporate exit.

The 3M exit

In December 2022, 3M announced it would stop manufacturing all PFAS by the end of 2025 — a decision made amid major PFAS litigation, including a multibillion-dollar water-contamination settlement. Because 3M’s Novec and Fluorinert lines were the backbone of two-phase immersion fluid supply, that single move effectively removed the dominant source for the technology. The last orders were accepted in early 2025 and manufacturing has now ceased; remaining channel inventory is finite and rising in price. Replacement directions are in the Novec replacement guide.

The EU restriction

Beyond any one company, the EU is advancing the broadest chemical restriction in REACH history, covering thousands of PFAS substances across many sectors — electronics and energy among them. As of early 2026, ECHA’s Risk Assessment Committee and Socio-Economic Analysis Committee have both backed a restriction (with debate over how many time-limited derogations to allow). The next steps: the committees’ final opinions go to the European Commission, which is expected to propose rules around 2027, with application generally not expected before 2029. The United States is also tightening PFAS rules. For anyone specifying a fluid meant to last the life of a data center or vehicle program, that direction matters.

Why a "drop-in" may not be the end of the story

Several prominent Novec replacements — including PFPE fluids such as Galden — are themselves PFAS chemistry. They restore supply, but if you’re exposed to the coming EU restriction or future U.S. rules, they don’t resolve the regulatory question — they defer it. Whether that’s acceptable depends entirely on where you sell and how long the system must run.

What it means for your fluid choice

  • Two-phase commitments now carry fluid-supply risk — confirm a compliant, durable source before you architect around it.
  • PFAS-free generally means single-phase today — hydrocarbon, synthetic, or ester fluids, since mature PFAS-free two-phase fluids are still emerging.
  • Geography decides urgency — selling into the EU raises the stakes considerably, with a roughly 2029 application horizon to plan against.
  • Document the fluid’s PFAS status in writing as part of selection.

Frequently asked

Are all immersion fluids PFAS?
No — only fluorinated fluids. Hydrocarbon, synthetic, and ester fluids are PFAS-free, which is why much of the market is moving toward them.
When does the EU restriction take effect?
It’s still in process. ECHA’s committees backed a restriction in March 2026; the European Commission is expected to propose rules around 2027, with application generally not before 2029. Treat the direction as clear and the exact dates as something to verify against current ECHA guidance.
Does PFAS-free mean worse cooling?
Not for most applications. Single-phase PFAS-free fluids cool very effectively for the majority of data-center and EV needs. The clearest performance gap is at the extreme densities where two-phase boiling’s latent-heat advantage matters most.

The short answer

3M stopped manufacturing its Novec and Fluorinert engineered fluids at the end of 2025. If your two-phase immersion or thermal-management system depended on them, you have two paths: a fluorinated drop-in replacement (keeps your system working, but is usually still PFAS), or a move to a PFAS-free chemistry (often single-phase). Which is right depends on your regulatory exposure and timeline — not on which vendor shouts loudest.

For years, two-phase immersion cooling and a range of electronics thermal-management designs were built around a small family of 3M fluids — principally Novec 7100, 7200, 7500, and 649, and the older Fluorinert liquids such as FC-72. They were prized for being non-conductive, non-flammable, low-viscosity, and chemically inert. Then the supply chain changed almost overnight.

What happened, and the dates that matter

On December 20, 2022, 3M announced it would exit all PFAS manufacturing by the end of 2025, citing tightening regulation and major litigation. That decision covered the entire Novec and Fluorinert range. The deadlines have now passed:

The phase-out window — and why it doesn’t end in 2025

The fork in the road: two honest paths

Almost every "Novec replacement" pitch falls into one of two categories. Knowing which you’re being sold matters, because they solve different problems.

Suppliers offer fluids engineered to match the boiling point and key properties of specific Novec or Fluorinert grades, so they slot into an existing two-phase system with minimal redesign — for example PFPE fluids (such as Galden) and distributor "drop-in" lines like BestSolv and others. The catch: many of these are themselves PFAS chemistry. They solve your supply problem but not your regulatory one — if you’re exposed to the EU restriction, a PFAS drop-in defers the same problem.

The other path is to step away from fluorinated fluids entirely. In practice this often means reconsidering the architecture — many PFAS-free options are single-phase (hydrocarbon, synthetic, or ester fluids pumped to a heat exchanger), since mature PFAS-free two-phase fluids are still emerging. It’s more design work up front, but it removes the regulatory question for the life of the system.

A pricing reality check

Fluid is a real line item. Engineered single-phase fluids commonly run on the order of $150–$400 per gallon depending on brand and purity, while basic mineral oils are far cheaper (roughly $20–$40 per gallon). Remaining Novec inventory is scarce and climbing. Across a full system’s fluid volume, this difference is material — factor it into the path decision.

How to choose, in four questions

  1. What’s your PFAS exposure? If you sell into the EU, or your customers have PFAS-free mandates, a fluorinated drop-in may not be durable.
  2. Can you change the architecture? If you can move from two-phase to single-phase, the PFAS-free option set opens up considerably.
  3. What’s your timeline? A drop-in buys time fast; a re-architecture takes longer but resolves the regulatory question.
  4. What are your hard performance limits? Extreme heat loads that genuinely need two-phase boiling narrow your options — a real constraint to weigh against compliance risk.

Frequently asked

Are Novec fluids really gone for good?
3M ended manufacturing of its PFAS-based Novec and Fluorinert products at the end of 2025, with last orders accepted in March 2025. Remaining channel inventory is finite and rising in price. Treat them as discontinued and plan a transition.
Is a "drop-in replacement" still PFAS?
Frequently, yes. Many drop-ins — including PFPE fluids such as Galden — are engineered to match Novec performance and are themselves fluorinated. They restore supply but carry the same regulatory exposure. Confirm the chemistry, not just the performance match.
Can I just switch to single-phase instead?
Often, yes — and for many data-center and electronics applications it’s the cleaner long-term answer, using PFAS-free hydrocarbon or synthetic fluids. The tradeoff is some redesign and, for the most extreme heat loads, a performance ceiling versus two-phase boiling. See single vs two-phase.
Will PFAS-free two-phase fluids arrive?
Suppliers are actively developing them, but mature, widely-validated PFAS-free two-phase fluids are still emerging. If you must stay two-phase and PFAS-free, track this closely with suppliers.
